title: Symplectic form, Darboux coordinates, and Hamiltonian fields
notes: The notes take a closed nondegenerate two-form \(\omega\) on a \(2n\)-manifold, write \(\omega=\sum dp_j\wedge dq_j\), and identify vector fields and one-forms. The coordinate identification and the names of locally Hamiltonian and Hamiltonian fields are not consistent with the displayed contraction.
statement: On a smooth symplectic manifold the map \(X\mapsto\iota_X\omega\) is an isomorphism. A vector field preserves \(\omega\) exactly when \(d\iota_X\omega=0\); it is Hamiltonian, in a stated sign convention, when that one-form is globally exact. Darboux coordinates exist locally, and \(\omega^n/n!\) is a nonvanishing volume form.
fate: These are established symplectic preliminaries in \citet[geometric preliminaries]{kostant1970quantization}, published in 1970; the seminar is expository here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the distinction between local closedness and global exactness remains essential. The obstruction to a symplectic field being Hamiltonian is its class in \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\).
reconstruction: Use the usual unnormalised exterior product and state a contraction sign explicitly; this changes the notebook’s coordinate signs and absorbs its factor of two.

title: Poisson bracket and the normalization problem
notes: The notebook sets \(dF=2\alpha_{\xi_F}\), defines \(\{F,G\}=\xi_FG\), and also identifies this with \(2\omega(\xi_F,\xi_G)\). It explicitly allows a wedge convention with \((dp\wedge dq)(\partial_p,\partial_q)=1/2\).
statement: Fix \(\iota_{X_f}\omega=-df\) and \(\{f,g\}=X_fg\). Then \(\{f,g\}=\omega(X_f,X_g)\), the bracket is a Lie bracket and a derivation in each argument, and \([X_f,X_g]=X_{\{f,g\}}\). These identities must all use the same normalization.
fate: The Poisson Lie algebra is part of the prequantization framework already developed in \citet{kostant1970quantization}. The discrepancy is internal to the recorded formulas, not a later mathematical obstruction.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is standard; the notebook’s simultaneous sign and normalization choices cannot be adopted literally without alteration.
reconstruction: The displayed convention is an editorial normalization, not a claim about Kirillov’s exact intended sign.

title: Integral symplectic forms and prequantum line bundles
notes: Local primitives \(\alpha_j\), differences \(df_{jk}\), integral triple overlaps, and transition functions \(e^{2\pi i f_{jk}}\) construct a line bundle.
statement: A closed real two-form \(\omega\) is the curvature class of a Hermitian line bundle with unitary connection of curvature \(-2\pi i\omega\) if and only if \([\omega]\) lies in the image of \(H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M;\mathbb R)\). Local potentials and a good cover give the Čech construction.
fate: This is the prequantization integrality criterion of \citet{kostant1970quantization}, published before the talk. The notes’ line-bundle construction is an exact conceptual match.
present_status: As of November 2026, the theorem is established. Torsion in integral cohomology is invisible to the de Rham class and contributes to the choice of prequantization.

title: Ambiguity of prequantization and flat twists
notes: The ambiguity in the line-bundle construction is described using \(H^1(X,\mathbb C^*)\).
statement: Isomorphism classes of line bundles with connection of a fixed curvature, when nonempty, form a torsor for flat line bundles with connection. In the unitary setting this group is \(H^1(M;\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\), equivalently homomorphisms \(\pi_1(M)\to U(1)\); for complex flat connections use the locally constant sheaf \(\mathbb C^*\).
fate: The ambiguity is part of the classification in \citet{kostant1970quantization}. The sheaf and connection data are necessary to interpret the abbreviated notation.
present_status: As of November 2026, one must not confuse this torsor with the classification of bare smooth complex line bundles by \(H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\).
reconstruction: The constant-sheaf interpretation and the distinction between unitary and general complex flat bundles are supplied explicitly.

title: The prequantum representation by first-order operators
notes: Compatible scalar first-order operators are expressed through a connection and multiplication. The notes give \(D_\varphi=\nabla_{\xi_\varphi}+\pi i\varphi\) and a Poisson commutator formula.
statement: With \(\iota_{X_f}\omega=-df\) and \(F_\nabla=-2\pi i\omega\), the operators \(D_f=\nabla_{X_f}+2\pi i f\) satisfy \([D_f,D_g]=D_{\{f,g\}}\). They are first-order operators on smooth sections of the prequantum line bundle; suitable domain and completeness assumptions are needed to exponentiate to group representations.
fate: \citet{kostant1970quantization} develops this representation before the seminar. The notebook explicitly cites the 1970 lecture volume; it is not an unpublished new quantization theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the Lie-algebra representation is standard, while its analytic integration and the choice of a smaller quantum space are separate questions.
reconstruction: The coefficients in the modern formula follow the normalization fixed in item 1971-229.2. No literal equality with the notebook’s \(\pi i\) convention is asserted.

title: Real, complex, and mixed polarizations
notes: A polarization is an involutive complex Lagrangian distribution \(F\). The cases \(F=\bar F\) and \(F\cap\bar F=0\) are called real and Kähler; mixed polarizations require a constant-rank condition. A sphere is said not to admit a global polarization.
statement: A regular polarization is a complex rank-\(n\) involutive Lagrangian subbundle of \(T_\mathbb C M\). A Kähler polarization additionally has the appropriate definiteness of \(i\omega(v,\bar v)\). On \(S^2\), no nonsingular real line-field polarization exists, but the standard complex structure gives a Kähler polarization.
fate: Polarizations and their use in quantization are developed in \citet{kostant1970quantization}. The sphere remark is correct only for nonsingular real polarizations, not for all complex polarizations.
present_status: As of November 2026, positivity, regularity, and the possible singularities of a real polarization must be specified. Transversality to the conjugate distribution alone gives a compatible complex structure, not positivity.
reconstruction: The restriction of the sphere claim to the real case is inferred from its local context and is flagged rather than silently supplied.

title: Polarized sections and the Poisson normalizer
notes: The quantum space is written \(\Gamma(L,F)=\{s:\nabla_Xs=0\text{ for }X\in F\}\). Leafwise constant functions form a locally maximal Poisson-commutative algebra \(A(F)\); its normalizer acts by first-order operators.
statement: For a regular real polarization, locally in a foliated Darboux chart, \(A(F)\) is maximal Poisson-commutative. If \(X_f\) preserves \(F\), the prequantum operator \(D_f\) preserves polarized sections. This preservation condition is locally equivalent to \(\{f,A(F)\}\subset A(F)\). Global maximality requires enough global first integrals and is not automatic.
fate: This is the standard polarization-preserving observable construction of \citet{kostant1970quantization}. The notebook itself qualifies maximal commutativity by \emph{locally}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the geometric statement is established. Global polarized sections may be too small or vanish, and half-form and Hilbert-space choices are additional structures, not supplied by this page.

title: Vertical polarization on a cotangent bundle
notes: For the distribution \(dq=0\), functions of \(q\) act by multiplication and functions linear in \(p\) give first-order operators.
statement: On \(T^*Q\) with its vertical real polarization, local polarized sections depend only on \(q\). The functions preserving this polarization are locally \(f(q,p)=a^j(q)p_j+b(q)\); their prequantum operators descend to first-order differential operators on \(Q\), with constants and signs fixed by the chosen connection.
fate: This Schrödinger-model example is part of the earlier construction in \citet{kostant1970quantization}. The affine, rather than strictly homogeneous linear, dependence on \(p\) includes multiplication operators.
present_status: As of November 2026, the local assertion is standard; a global measure or half-density convention determines the additional divergence term in a symmetric operator realization.

title: Regular unipotents and the singular locus in type A
notes: For \(SL_n(\mathbb C)\), one Jordan block gives a nonsingular point of the variety \(R\) of unipotent elements; several blocks give singular points. The \(SL_2\) example is a quadratic cone with vertex at the identity.
statement: For \(G=SL_n(\mathbb C)\), the unipotent variety is isomorphic by \(u\mapsto u-I\) to the nilpotent cone in \(\mathfrak{sl}_n\). Its smooth locus is the regular nilpotent orbit, equivalently the matrices with a single Jordan block. In \(SL_2\), writing \(a=1+x,d=1-x\) gives \(x^2+bc=0\).
fate: The regularity framework precedes the seminar: \citet[Theorems 1.1--1.5]{steinberg1965regular}; the notebook applies it in type A. The complex quadratic cone is a complex surface, not literally a real two-dimensional cone.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is a standard established description. The restriction to \(\mathbb C\) avoids inseparability and bad-characteristic issues hidden by the notebook’s broader comment.

title: Springer’s resolution by invariant complete flags
notes: Pairs \((p,g)\), where \(p\in B\backslash G\) and \(pgp^{-1}\in U\), define \(\widetilde R\to R\); the source is smooth and the generic fibre is one point. The margin calls \(B\backslash G\) projective space.
statement: For \(G=SL_n(\mathbb C)\), let \(\mathcal B\) be the complete flag variety and \(\widetilde R=\{(u,F_\bullet):uF_i\subset F_i\}\). The projection to the unipotent variety is proper and birational, and \(\widetilde R\simeq G\times^B U\) is smooth. A regular unipotent has a unique invariant complete flag. The base is a projective variety, generally not a projective space.
fate: This is the resolution in \citet{springer1969unipotent}, an account from the 1968 Bombay colloquium published in 1969. The original chapter was not obtained; its identity is corroborated by later primary papers, while the construction here is independently checked as an associated bundle.
present_status: As of November 2026, the type-A construction is established. An assertion over every field should be phrased as a geometric morphism after base change, not as a resolution by sets of rational points.

title: Invariant flag counts and Hall polynomials
notes: The number of flags over \(\mathbb F_q\) is polynomial in \(q\); for a unipotent \(g\), the fixed-flag count depends only on its Jordan partition. Green’s 1955 character paper is recommended.
statement: The number of complete flags in \(\mathbb F_q^n\) is \(\prod_{j=1}^n(1+q+\cdots+q^{j-1})\). For a nilpotent operator of fixed Jordan type \(\lambda\), its invariant complete flags are counted by a polynomial in \(q\). It can be computed by successive Hall-number counts of submodules of the corresponding \(\mathbb F_q[t]\)-module; the total count need not be identified with one unspecified Hall polynomial.
fate: The Hall-polynomial and finite-general-linear-group connection was already available in \citet{green1955characters}. A later geometric verification through affine decompositions is read in \citet[Introduction and \S1]{shimomura1980fixed}. Green’s full text was not successfully opened in this run.
present_status: As of November 2026, the counting assertion is established. The field-independent Jordan type and the choice of complete rather than partial flags must be fixed.

title: Flag counts and the even Poincaré polynomial
notes: The notes compare the finite-field polynomial with the Poincaré polynomial after replacing \(q\) by \(t^2\).
statement: The complex full flag variety has an affine Bruhat decomposition with cells \(\mathbb C^{\ell(w)}\), \(w\in S_n\). Thus its cohomology is concentrated in even degrees and \(P(t)=\sum_wt^{2\ell(w)}\), while its split finite-field model has \(\sum_wq^{\ell(w)}\) points. A corresponding comparison for invariant-flag varieties requires a compatible affine paving, not an arbitrary variety whose point count happens to be polynomial.
fate: The full-flag comparison is classical. The later explicit invariant-flag decomposition of \citet[\S1]{shimomura1980fixed} substantiates the stronger type-A comparison; the paper credits Spaltenstein’s 1976 complete-flag result.
present_status: As of November 2026, the full-flag statement and the type-A Springer-fibre analogue are established. The notebook does not record a general theorem equating arbitrary point counts and Betti numbers.

title: Dimension of a Springer fibre and the centralizer
notes: The fibre dimension is bounded above by \(\tfrac12(\dim Z_g-(n-1))\).
statement: For unipotent \(u\in SL_n(\mathbb C)\), \(\dim\mathcal B_u=\tfrac12(\dim Z_{SL_n}(u)-(n-1))\). If the Jordan partition is \(\lambda\), this is \(\sum_i(i-1)\lambda_i\). In \(GL_n\), replace \(n-1\) by \(n\), since the centralizer dimension also increases by one.
fate: The notebook’s upper bound belongs to Springer’s earlier geometry \citep{springer1969unipotent}; later fixed-flag work supplies sharper structural descriptions \citep[Introduction]{shimomura1980fixed}. The exact original locator for the upper bound was not retrieved, so the historical match is indirect.
present_status: As of November 2026, the equality in type A is established. The rank term is group-dependent; mixing a \(GL_n\) centralizer with the \(SL_n\) rank gives an incorrect half-integer formula.

title: The unlocated Rego note on cohomology and integrable distributions
notes: The heading says Rosenfeld reports on Rego, \emph{C. R.}, volume 272 (1971), and associates cohomology with an integrable distribution. The author name is legible on the scan.
statement: The surviving text does not specify the cochain groups, differential, equivalence relation on distributions, or an exact theorem. It therefore does not determine a unique cohomology theory or a definite open problem.
fate: Searches combining Rego, volume 272, 1971, foliation/cohomology, and Frölicher--Nijenhuis terminology did not identify the cited note securely. The surrounding derivation calculus can be identified independently, but it does not justify assigning the missing theorem to a guessed author.
present_status: As of November 2026, the bibliographic identification remains unresolved in this bounded search. No assertion that the idea was undeveloped or remains open is warranted.

title: Decomposition of graded derivations and the Frölicher–Nijenhuis bracket
notes: The notes describe derivations of the graded algebra of forms by vector-valued forms and insertion. For a vector-valued \(p\)-form \(L\), they write \(d_L=d\,i_L+(-1)^p i_Ld\).
statement: Every degree-\(k\) graded derivation of \(\Omega^*(M)\) has a unique decomposition \(\mathcal L_K+i_L\), with \(K\in\Omega^k(M;TM)\), \(L\in\Omega^{k+1}(M;TM)\), and \(\mathcal L_K=[i_K,d]\). The commutator of Lie derivations defines \([K,H]_{FN}\) by \([\mathcal L_K,\mathcal L_H]=\mathcal L_{[K,H]_{FN}}\).
fate: This calculus is due to Frölicher and Nijenhuis in 1956. It is explicitly attributed and reviewed in the author’s account \citet[Introduction]{michor1989derivations}; the original 1956 publisher text was not accessible here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the decomposition is established. The notebook’s \(d_L\) equals \((-1)^p\mathcal L_L\) in this convention; that is a convention difference, not by itself a mathematical error.
reconstruction: The form degrees and graded commutator are supplied. For \(L=\operatorname{Id}_{TM}\), the notebook convention gives \(-d\), consistently with this sign conversion.

title: When an induced Lie derivation is a differential
notes: The short entry links the construction with integrability and a cohomology, without specifying a degree or a torsion identity.
statement: For a vector-valued one-form \(N\), \(\mathcal L_N^2=\tfrac12\mathcal L_{[N,N]_{FN}}\). Hence vanishing Nijenhuis torsion gives a degree-one differential. An arbitrary graded Lie derivation does not automatically square to zero; a foliation gives a leafwise de Rham differential by a different, explicitly specified construction.
fate: The precise graded identity belongs to the Frölicher--Nijenhuis calculus reviewed in \citet[\S\S1--2]{michor1989derivations}; \citet{michor1987remarks} gives a broader account. The relation of this identity to the unidentified Rego announcement is only a reconstruction, not an exact publication match.
present_status: As of November 2026, the torsion-zero implication is standard. Which of these complexes Rosenfeld intended cannot be decided from this page alone.
reconstruction: The vector-valued one-form formulation is a mathematically valid interpretation, not a recovered missing theorem.

title: The critical exponent of a finite-dimensional norm
notes: The notes define an exponent \(q\) by \(\|A\|=\|A^q\|=1\Rightarrow r(A)=1\), together with a counterexample for \(q-1\). The dimension sign is visually ambiguous between finite dimension and \(\le\infty\).
statement: For a finite-dimensional real or complex normed space \(E\), let \(q(E)\) be the least positive integer \(q\), if it exists, such that every contraction \(A\) with \(\|A^q\|=1\) has spectral radius one; otherwise set \(q(E)=\infty\). For \(q>1\), minimality gives a contraction \(B\) with \(\|B^{q-1}\|=1\) and \(r(B)<1\). In dimension one, \(q(E)=1\), and the notebook’s additional requirement \(\|B\|=1\) cannot be imposed on a predecessor witness.
fate: The definition and equivalent eventual-norm-drop formulation are given in \citet[p.~672]{kirzhnertabachnikov1971critical}, referring to earlier work of Pták and Mařík. It predates this September talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the finite-dimensional invariant is well defined with the stated convention. An infinite-dimensional extension requires care: spectral radius, spectral values, and norm-attainment arguments cannot simply be copied.
reconstruction: Finite dimension and the dimension-one exception are explicit editorial qualifications.

title: Critical exponent of a Hilbert space
notes: The table gives \(q(\ell_2^n)=n\).
statement: For a real or complex Hilbert space of finite dimension \(n\), every contraction \(A\) with \(\|A^n\|=1\) has spectral radius one, and the exponent is sharp. For \(n\ge2\), a nilpotent shift has \(\|A^{n-1}\|=1\) and \(A^n=0\); dimension one is immediate.
fate: This was Pták’s 1962 result, cited on p.~672 of \citet{kirzhnertabachnikov1971critical}. \citet[\S\S1--2]{ptak1976isometric} gives a later proof by isometric parts. The 1976 date is not the date the theorem first became known.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exact exponent is established. The Hilbert geometry is essential; an arbitrary norm on the same vector space may have a different exponent or no finite one.

title: Critical exponents of the one and infinity norms
notes: The table gives \(q(\ell_1^n)=q(\ell_\infty^n)=n^2-n+1\).
statement: For the usual \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms in dimension \(n\), the critical exponent is \(n^2-n+1\), with the predecessor-witness convention separately understood for \(n=1\). Duality identifies the two exponents because \(\|(A^*)^j\|=\|A^j\|\) and \(r(A^*)=r(A)\).
fate: \citet[p.~672]{kirzhnertabachnikov1971critical} explicitly records these established values and their earlier references. Thus they were not new in September 1971; the historical source for the exact maximum-norm result is earlier work of Mařík and Pták.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exact values are established. They demonstrate why dimension alone does not determine the exponent.

title: A two-dimensional norm with no finite critical exponent
notes: The notebook attributes an example to Danzer and sketches a unit ball with rotations by small angles; it asserts \(q(E)=\infty\) in dimension two.
statement: There exists a real two-dimensional normed space for which, for every integer \(m\), a contraction \(A_m\) has \(\|A_m^m\|=1\) but \(r(A_m)<1\). A bare rotation has spectral radius one and is not by itself such a witness; the norm geometry and the contracting linear map must be specified.
fate: \citet[example, pp.~674--675]{kirzhnertabachnikov1971critical} gives an explicit two-dimensional example using a piecewise algebraic unit sphere and diagonal contracting maps. This verifies the existence claim before the talk, but it does not identify the notebook’s Danzer diagram or its attribution.
present_status: As of November 2026, the existence of infinite critical exponent in dimension two is established. The exact Danzer construction remains an unresolved bibliographic detail, not an open existence problem.

title: Finiteness for finite-dimensional lp spaces
notes: The notes say existence of a critical exponent for \(\ell_p^n\) is unknown except for \(p=2^m\), and call it useful for numerical analysis.
statement: For each fixed dimension \(n\) and \(1\le p<\infty\), ask whether \(q(\ell_p^n)<\infty\), specifying real or complex scalars. A verified partial answer is affirmative for every rational \(p\): if the unit sphere lies in a real algebraic zero set not containing the origin, a finite exponent exists, and rational-\(p\) spheres satisfy that criterion.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1 and Corollaries 2--3]{kirzhnertabachnikov1971critical}, received 14 January 1970 and printed May--June 1971, proves rational-\(p\) finiteness over both scalar fields. The notebook’s state-of-knowledge claim is already obsolete on its catalogue date. Searches through November 2026 did not verify an exact all-real-\(p\) successor or optimal general exponents.
present_status: As of November 2026, rational-\(p\) finiteness is established. The status of the remaining irrational parameters and sharp quantitative values was not established by this bounded search; this is not a certification that they are open today.
worth: A focused follow-up is worthwhile to identify the exact irrational-\(p\) literature and sharpen an explicitly chosen finite-dimensional case; the algebraic proof itself is already published.

title: Does the minimum critical exponent tend to infinity with dimension?
notes: The notes define \(M(n)\) as the minimum over norms, report \(M(n)\le n\), examples below \(n\), and a subsequence on the scale \(\sqrt n\), and ask whether \(\liminf M(n)=\infty\).
statement: Fix the scalar field and define \(M(n)=\min\{q(E):\dim E=n\}\), using \(q(E)=\infty\) when necessary. The Hilbert norm gives \(M(n)\le n\). The definite question is whether, for every integer \(K\), only finitely many dimensions admit a norm with \(q(E)\le K\). The notebook’s subsequence claim is a separate reported bound whose precise construction was not located.
fate: Pták’s Hilbert result verifies the basic upper bound \citep{ptak1976isometric}. Bilingual searches of critical exponents, minimum over norms, and \(M(n)\) did not establish the exact later fate. The 1995 literature on \emph{exponential numbers} uses a different orbit-growth invariant and cannot be substituted for this contraction exponent.
present_status: As of November 2026, the historical question is precise, and some special-space bounds are established, but its exact current resolution remains unverified here. Class C records that partial development and unresolved identification, not a proof of present-day openness.
worth: It is worth first recovering the precise norm construction behind the reported \(\sqrt n\) subsequence; without that bibliographic step a new asymptotic claim would risk duplicating or misidentifying existing work.

title: The twelve-dimensional direct-sum example is not securely reconstructible
notes: The scan writes a sum rendered \(\ell_4^2\oplus_{\ell_1}\ell_8^2\), followed by dimension 12 and critical exponent 11.
statement: With the conventional notation \(\ell_p^n\), the displayed sum has dimension four, not twelve. Swapping the roles of superscript and subscript would give Hilbert spaces of dimensions four and eight, but this reading is not established by the scan and its exponent must not be inferred. A unique normed space and claimed exact exponent cannot presently be assigned.
fate: The direct-sum construction was not located securely in the searched Pták literature. The preceding discussion of \(M(n)<n\) makes it plausible that a twelve-dimensional example was intended, but plausibility does not resolve the notation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the example remains unidentified. Neither the exponent 11 for the literal four-dimensional space nor a proposed repaired twelve-dimensional space is claimed verified.

title: The constrained power-norm extremum
notes: The page defines \(C(E,r,\rho)=\max\{\|T^r\|:\|T\|\le1,\ r(T)\le\rho\}\), with \(0<\rho<1\).
statement: \ours\ For finite-dimensional \(E\), integer \(r\ge1\), and \(0\le\rho<1\), the admissible set is compact, so this maximum exists. If \(q(E)<\infty\) and \(r\ge q(E)\), then \(C(E,r,\rho)<1\) for every fixed \(\rho<1\). Conversely, if \(r<q(E)\), some \(\rho<1\) gives \(C(E,r,\rho)=1\). Determining exact values and maximizers is a quantitative problem depending on the norm, dimension, \(r\), and \(\rho\).
fate: The extremal viewpoint is part of Pták’s programme; the critical-exponent results in \citet{ptak1976isometric} concern its qualitative threshold. The compactness implication stated here is an elementary editorial deduction, not a claim that the full optimization has been solved. Searches did not identify a uniform exact solution for arbitrary norms.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualitative finite-dimensional relation to \(q(E)\) is clear. Exact general values and the complete later classification of extremizers were not verified in this run; no blanket open-problem claim is made.
worth: For a specified low-dimensional norm and fixed spectral-radius bound, a certified optimization or sharp estimate could be a bounded contribution; the unrestricted problem is too broad for a defensible new result here.
reconstruction: \ours\ Compactness, continuity of spectral radius, and attainment justify the maximum and strict inequality; these hypotheses and deductions are supplied explicitly.

title: Affine finite-field Radon inversion by incidence counting
notes: For \(f:\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\), \(\varphi(p)\) sums \(f\) over a \emph{plane}. Counting planes through one or two points yields an inversion identity.
statement: Let \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal H\) be all affine hyperplanes of \(V=\mathbb F_q^n\), and set \(Rf(H)=\sum_{x\in H}f(x)\). Put \(b=(q^{n-1}-1)/(q-1)\) and \(C=\sum_Vf\). Then \(\sum_{H\ni x}Rf(H)=q^{n-1}f(x)+bC\), so \(f(x)=q^{1-n}(\sum_{H\ni x}Rf(H)-bC)\). \ours\ The count uses \((q^n-1)/(q-1)\) hyperplanes through one point and \(b\) through two distinct points.
fate: The identity is verified directly from the incidence counts on the page. Related finite integral geometry was developed in \citet[Theorems 1--2]{graevpavlenko1972radon}, submitted February 1972, for projective spaces over finite commutative rings; that is a related generalization, not an exact publication of this affine formula.
present_status: As of November 2026, the inversion formula is established and elementary. The exact first publication of this notebook formulation was not identified. The fate classification records the later developed subject, without assigning priority.
reconstruction: \ours\ \emph{Plane} means hyperplane, as forced by the numerical coefficients; function values are taken in characteristic zero so division by \(q\) is valid.

title: The range condition from parallel classes
notes: The sum of \(\varphi(p)\) over each parallel class is the same constant \(C\), called a finite analogue of a Paley--Wiener condition.
statement: Over \(\mathbb C\), the image of \(R\) consists exactly of functions \(\varphi\) on affine hyperplanes for which \(\sum_{H\parallel H_0}\varphi(H)\) is independent of the direction \(H_0\). \ours\ Necessity follows by partitioning \(V\). For sufficiency, there are \(a=(q^n-1)/(q-1)\) parallel classes, each of size \(q\); the \(a-1\) independent equal-sum constraints leave dimension \(aq-(a-1)=q^n\), equal to the domain dimension, and the preceding inversion proves injectivity.
fate: This is an editorial completion of the notebook’s elementary range observation. The projective transform in \citet{graevpavlenko1972radon} supplies related later development but has different range geometry; no exact source for this affine characterization was verified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the range characterization is proved by the displayed finite-dimensional argument. It is not an unresolved Paley--Wiener problem.
reconstruction: \ours\ The sufficiency proof and its dimension count are supplied here; the page explicitly records only the equal-sum condition.

title: Gaussian binomial coefficients and the limit q equals one
notes: A remark attributed to Rota interprets \(C_k^n(q)\) as the number of \(k\)-dimensional subspaces and states its limit is \(\binom nk\).
statement: The number of \(k\)-subspaces of \(\mathbb F_q^n\) is \(\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{k}_q=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(q^{n-j}-1)/(q^{k-j}-1)\), a polynomial in \(q\) with integer coefficients. Its polynomial value at \(q=1\), equivalently the limit of this rational expression, is \(\binom nk\). It is a polynomial specialization, not a finite field with one element.
fate: This finite-vector-space combinatorics is already developed in \citet{goldmanrota1970finite}, published September 1970, whose bibliography also records their 1969 subspace-count paper. Publisher metadata and references were checked; the collected full text exceeded the retrieval limit.
present_status: As of November 2026, the identity is established. It explains the numerical coefficients in the preceding Radon argument.

title: Microlocal regularity and the wavefront set
notes: For a distribution \(A\), the notes test \(\langle A,\varphi e^{it\psi}\rangle=o(t^{-N})\) for every \(N\), with \(d\psi\) prescribed at one point and arbitrary compactly supported \(\varphi\). Smooth functions have empty wavefront.
statement: For \(u\in\mathcal D^{\prime}(M)\), a nonzero covector \((x_0,\xi_0)\) is outside \(\operatorname{WF}(u)\) if, in a coordinate chart, there is a cutoff equal to one near \(x_0\) whose Fourier transform after multiplication by \(u\) decreases faster than every power in an open conic neighbourhood of \(\xi_0\). The wavefront is closed, conic, and projects to the singular support.
fate: \citet[\S2.5]{hormander1971fourier} gives the contemporary definition and calculus. The article was printed on 1 June 1971 and developed material circulated in the 1969 Nordic summer-school lectures, before this September talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the definition is standard. The notebook’s condition requires sufficiently small support and uniform control in neighbouring phase directions; requiring arbitrary support while prescribing \(d\psi\) only at one point is not a valid literal criterion.

title: Conormal bundles as Lagrangians
notes: A submanifold \(N\subset M\) gives the normal bundle of annihilating covectors, described as a Lagrangian of half the cotangent dimension.
statement: For an embedded smooth submanifold \(N\), its conormal bundle \(N^*M=\{(x,\xi):x\in N,\xi|_{T_xN}=0\}\) is Lagrangian in \(T^*M\). The wavefront of a conormal distribution lies in \(N^*M\setminus0\); the Dirac density along a smooth submanifold has precisely this wavefront when its density is nonvanishing.
fate: The conormal model is a basic case of the oscillatory constructions in \citet[\S1 and \S3]{hormander1971fourier}. It was established before the seminar.
present_status: As of November 2026, the assertion is standard; \emph{normal} here means conormal covectors, without choosing a Riemannian metric.

title: Pseudodifferential kernels are conormal to the diagonal
notes: A pseudodifferential operator is described as a distribution kernel on \(M\times M\) whose wavefront is constructed from the diagonal.
statement: The Schwartz kernel of a properly supported pseudodifferential operator of finite order belongs locally to a conormal distribution class for the diagonal; in particular \(\operatorname{WF}(K)\subset N^*\Delta\setminus0\). Wavefront containment alone is not a characterization of the symbol class or of finite operator order.
fate: The symbol hypotheses and oscillatory kernel definition are present in \citet[Definition 1.1.1 and the pseudodifferential sections]{hormander1971fourier}. The notebook records the geometric support of singularities but omits their quantitative order.
present_status: As of November 2026, the inclusion is established. A converse needs symbol estimates or equivalent iterated regularity conditions.

title: Oscillatory parametrization of a Lagrangian distribution
notes: The page states that every distribution with wavefront in a Lagrangian is given by an oscillatory integral, and writes a phase-gradient description of \(\Lambda\).
statement: A nondegenerate phase \(\phi(x,\theta)\), homogeneous of degree one in \(\theta\), parametrizes \(\Lambda=\{(x,d_x\phi):d_\theta\phi=0\}\). Integrating \(e^{i\phi}a\) against a symbol \(a\) yields a Lagrangian distribution. Membership in \(I^m(M,\Lambda)\) entails amplitude estimates and is strictly stronger than the bare inclusion \(\operatorname{WF}(u)\subset\Lambda\). Locally, members of this class have such representations modulo smooth functions.
fate: \citet[\S3]{hormander1971fourier} establishes the phase and amplitude calculus. The notebook collapses the quantitative class condition into a wavefront condition, so its literal universal converse is not the theorem of that paper.
present_status: As of November 2026, the appropriately qualified theorem is established. No new classification problem is inferred from the missing hypotheses.
reconstruction: The stationary equations \(d_\theta\phi=0\) and the symbol class are supplied; they are essential, not cosmetic.

title: The Godbillon–Vey three-class
notes: For an integrable defining one-form \(\omega\), choose \(\omega_1,\omega_2\) with \(d\omega=\omega\wedge\omega_1\), \(d\omega_1=\omega\wedge\omega_2\); the closed form \(\Omega=\omega\wedge\omega_1\wedge\omega_2\) defines a choice-independent class.
statement: For a smooth cooriented codimension-one foliation, take a nowhere-vanishing defining form \(\omega\) and a one-form \(\eta\) with \(d\omega=\omega\wedge\eta\). The form \(\eta\wedge d\eta\) is closed and its de Rham class is independent of the choices. With the notebook convention, \(\Omega=-\eta\wedge d\eta\); this overall sign must be fixed when comparing numerical invariants.
fate: \citet[\S1]{godbillonvey1971invariant} introduced the class in the issue dated 12 July 1971. Bernstein’s 20 September report is therefore exposition of a published result, not a later 1972 discovery.
present_status: As of November 2026, the smooth construction is established. Compactness is needed to integrate over a fundamental cycle, not to define the cohomology class.

title: Vanishing for a foliation by fibres
notes: The class is zero when the foliation is a fibration.
statement: For a cooriented codimension-one foliation given by the fibres of a smooth submersion onto an oriented one-dimensional manifold, a nowhere-zero closed defining one-form can be chosen by pulling back a one-form on the base. Taking \(\eta=0\) makes the Godbillon--Vey form zero.
fate: This is a special case of \citet[\S2(i)]{godbillonvey1971invariant}: a nonsingular closed Pfaffian defining form gives zero class. The result predates the talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the fibre-foliation assertion is established with the indicated global defining-form hypothesis.

title: Deformation invariance versus foliated concordance
notes: The notebook says \ru{устойчив при деформ.}, stable under deformations, with no qualification on the deformation.
statement: The Godbillon--Vey class is natural and invariant under a foliated concordance on \(M\times[0,1]\) transverse to the boundary. It need not be constant along an arbitrary smooth parameter family of foliations on \(M\). Thurston’s polygon construction yields foliations of \(S^3\) whose integrated classes vary as \(4\pi\operatorname{Area}(P)\), up to orientation convention.
fate: The original \citet[\S1(iii)]{godbillonvey1971invariant} uses differentiable homotopy of foliations, which must be interpreted in its foliation-theoretic sense. \citet[p.~513]{thurston1972noncobordant}, communicated 15 December 1971 and published in 1972, demonstrates variable values. This refutes an unrestricted reading of the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, unrestricted deformation invariance is false. A path of integrable plane fields is weaker than an integrable foliation on the product giving a concordance.

title: The nonzero homogeneous example on a compact SL2 quotient
notes: The page sketches a compact quotient of \(SL_2(\mathbb R)\) by a discrete subgroup and the foliation by triangular-subgroup orbits, asserting dense trajectories and a nonzero class.
statement: For a cocompact lattice \(\Gamma\subset SL_2(\mathbb R)\), the foliation on \(\Gamma\backslash SL_2(\mathbb R)\) associated to a two-dimensional Borel subgroup has a Godbillon--Vey form which is a nonzero invariant volume form. Hence its integral, with an orientation, is nonzero. Left/right quotient and invariant-form conventions must be made compatible.
fate: This is Roussarie’s example recorded explicitly in \citet[\S2(iii)]{godbillonvey1971invariant}. Thus the nonzero example was published before Bernstein’s report. The page’s separate density assertion is not required for computing the class.
present_status: As of November 2026, the homogeneous nonvanishing is established. The word \emph{always} about density is meaningful only with the compact quotient and the intended connected orbit foliation fixed; it is not a statement for every discrete subgroup.

title: Transverse pseudogroups and formal vector-field characteristic classes
notes: Local submersions \(\varphi_i\) give transition maps on intervals; because they form a pseudogroup rather than a single finite-dimensional group, the talk turns to \(W_1\), formal vector fields on the line.
statement: A codimension-one foliation admits a Haefliger cocycle \(\varphi_j=\psi_{ji}\circ\varphi_i\) on sufficiently small overlaps, where the \(\psi_{ji}\) are local diffeomorphisms of intervals. Formal transverse jets yield a characteristic homomorphism from the appropriate continuous formal-vector-field cohomology to de Rham cohomology of the foliated manifold.
fate: The original \citet[\S3]{godbillonvey1971invariant} constructs a universal Lie coalgebra for this purpose. The broader formal-coordinate construction is developed in the contemporary \citet{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry} and is discussed in record 243.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established source of secondary foliation classes. The raw composition \(\varphi_j\varphi_i\) on the page is not defined; the overlap factorization is the correct relation.
reconstruction: The term Haefliger cocycle and the explicit factorization specify the modern meaning of the sketch.

title: The continuous cohomology of W1
notes: The page says the cohomology vanishes except for \(H^3(W_1;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R\), identifying that generator with the preceding class.
statement: For the Lie algebra \(W_1\) of formal vector fields in one variable with its formal topology and trivial coefficients, continuous cohomology is one-dimensional in degrees 0 and 3 and zero in other degrees. The degree-three generator induces the Godbillon--Vey class under the characteristic map.
fate: The formal-vector-field computation belongs to \citet{gelfandfuchs1970formal}; \citet[\S3]{godbillonvey1971invariant} identifies the foliation class. The missing degree-zero copy is an omitted standard qualification.
present_status: As of November 2026, the cohomology statement is established for continuous cochains. It does not assert the same result for arbitrary discontinuous algebraic cochains.

title: Discrete spectrum of a self-adjoint elliptic operator
notes: On a compact manifold, a self-adjoint elliptic differential operator has a discrete real spectrum, with positive and negative eigenvalues.
statement: On a closed smooth manifold, a formally self-adjoint elliptic differential operator of positive order on a Hermitian vector bundle has a self-adjoint realization with compact resolvent. Its eigenvalues are real, have finite multiplicities, and accumulate only at infinity. There need not be infinitely many eigenvalues of both signs; boundary problems require boundary conditions.
fate: These spectral facts are older elliptic theory, used as preliminaries in \citet[\S2]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3}; the 1976 paper is a verification source, not their first publication.
present_status: As of November 2026, the assertion is established with closedness or an appropriate elliptic boundary realization. Two-sided unbounded spectrum is an additional condition relevant to nontrivial loop examples.

title: Spectral flow for a closed self-adjoint family
notes: The eigenvalues move with \(t\), and the net number passing zero defines an integer. The family is periodic or closes by \(D_{t+1}=UD_tU^{-1}\).
statement: A continuous loop of self-adjoint Fredholm operators, in a topology supporting continuous spectral projections near zero, has an integer spectral flow counting negative-to-positive crossings with sign. For smooth elliptic families, it is invariant under homotopies of loops. For open paths, endpoint conditions or a specified endpoint convention are required.
fate: \citet[\S7, pp.~93--94]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3} defines and studies this invariant; the paper notes earlier joint work with Lusztig. The present September 1971 notebook is evidence of earlier seminar circulation; the published paper was received in January 1975 and appeared in 1976.
present_status: As of November 2026, spectral flow is established and applies beyond compact-resolvent differential operators. It must not be identified with an unsigned count of crossings.

title: The unit spectral-flow example on the circle
notes: The example is \(D_t=-i\,d/dx+t\), with \(Uf=e^{ix}f\), and the recorded flow is \(\pm1\).
statement: On the circle of length \(2\pi\), with periodic domain \(H^1\), the eigenvalues are \(n+t\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\). Over any unit interval with invertible endpoints, exactly one eigenvalue crosses upward, giving spectral flow \(+1\). Multiplication by \(e^{ix}\) satisfies \(UD_tU^{-1}=D_t-1\), so closure as written requires \(U=e^{-ix}\) or reversing the conjugation.
fate: The same spectral model \(n+t\) is given in \citet[p.~94]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3}. Its presence here is an early explicit example; the conjugation discrepancy is a faithful sign error in the notebook, independently checked by differentiating \(e^{-ix}f\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the example is exact after a consistent orientation and gluing convention. The alternative \(\pm1\) records convention, whereas the displayed conjugation formula must actually be changed.

title: Computing spectral flow from geometric data
notes: The stated problem is to compute spectral flow from the manifold, operator, and gluing \(U\). The proposed answer is the index of \(P=\partial_t+D_t\) on the mapping torus.
statement: Let \(D_t\) be a smooth family of self-adjoint first-order elliptic operators on the fibres of a smooth bundle over \(S^1\), acting on a compatibly glued Hermitian vector bundle. Then the suspended operator \(\partial_t+D_t\), with a connection in the parameter direction, is elliptic and \(\operatorname{sf}(D_t)=\operatorname{ind}(\partial_t+D_t)\). Equivalently spectral flow is the topological index of the family symbol. An arbitrary Hilbert-space unitary need not define such a geometric mapping torus.
fate: \citet[Theorem 7.4 and pp.~94--95]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3} proves precisely the topological formula and the first-order suspension equality, including a remark on nontrivial fibre bundles over the circle. This is a strong A identification, with 1971 circulation distinct from 1976 publication.
present_status: As of November 2026, the geometric computation problem is solved under the stated elliptic and gluing hypotheses. The general Fredholm-loop invariant remains meaningful when a local differential mapping-torus model is unavailable.

title: Analytic eigenvalue branches and the orbit heuristic
notes: Real-analytic dependence is used to label eigenvalues globally, and periodicity permutes their branches. Finite orbits and branches travelling towards the two infinities are used to read the integer. The bound \(|\lambda^{\prime}(t)|<C|\lambda(t)|\) is displayed.
statement: For an analytic self-adjoint elliptic family with common domain and uniform elliptic estimates, local real-analytic eigenvalue branches can be continued along the real parameter. Their derivatives obey an estimate of the form \(|\lambda^{\prime}(t)|\le C(1+|\lambda(t)|)\) on compact parameter intervals. The notebook’s homogeneous bound forbids a nonzero derivative at a zero crossing and is contradicted by its own branch \(\lambda(t)=t\).
fate: The later rigorous treatment in \citet[\S7]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3} defines spectral flow through spectral graphs and perturbation, without requiring the informal orbit classification to carry the proof. The branch sketch is an antecedent, not a complete published argument.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected analytic estimates support the spectral picture; the exact four-type orbit description needs hypotheses and is retained only as a heuristic. No general monotonicity of eigenvalues is implied.

title: The diagonal scalar-ODE model for the suspended index
notes: Assuming eigenvectors independent of \(t\), the solutions are \(u_n(t)=c_n\exp(-\int\lambda_n)\). The notes use orbit counts for \(\ker P\) and \(\ker P^*\), and write \(\int_0^N\lambda_n(t)dt=0\) for a finite orbit.
statement: In a diagonal model, \((\partial_t+\lambda(t))u=0\) gives \(u(t)=c\exp(-\int_0^t\lambda(s)ds)\). On a periodic orbit of length \(N\), a nonzero periodic solution exists exactly when the scalar monodromy is one; for real \(\lambda\), this is \(\int_0^N\lambda=0\). It is a condition, not an automatic identity. Such finite orbits contribute equally to kernel and cokernel. Infinite unfolded orbits require explicit square-integrability and gluing conditions.
fate: The notebook labels the calculation heuristic and acknowledges extra terms from moving eigenvectors. The rigorous equality is \citet[pp.~94--95]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3}; the displayed scalar model is only a special-case explanation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the elementary ODE calculation is valid with its boundary conditions, but does not by itself prove the general spectral-flow theorem.

title: A diffeomorphism and the obstruction from a natural operator family
notes: A diffeomorphism \(T:X\to X\), a metric, and a natural self-adjoint operator determine a family on the mapping torus. If \(T\) preserves a metric, the family is constant and its flow vanishes.
statement: For a diffeomorphism-equivariant elliptic construction, compatible endpoint identification and a path of metrics give a closed operator family. If the spectral-flow class is independent of that path and an invariant metric exists, one may use the constant metric, so the invariant is zero. Consequently a verified nonzero value obstructs an invariant metric; the conclusion is conditional on the operator family actually having nonzero possible flow.
fate: The mapping-torus extension appears in \citet[remark after Theorem 7.4]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3}. The notebook’s geometric observation is a correct application of homotopy invariance, but its next choice \(d+\delta\) requires a separate audit.
present_status: As of November 2026, the implication is valid for a suitably specified natural elliptic family. It does not establish that every suggested natural operator yields an effective obstruction.

title: The ungraded de Rham operator has zero spectral flow
notes: The example offered for the preceding construction is \(d+\delta\) on forms. No chirality restriction or odd-signature modification is written.
statement: On all differential forms, \(D_t=d_t+d_t^*\) anticommutes with degree parity \(\Gamma\omega=(-1)^{\deg\omega}\omega\). If the endpoint gluing preserves parity, a closed family is unitarily conjugate to its negative; spectral-flow invariance and sign reversal give \(\operatorname{sf}(D_t)=0\). A potentially nontrivial signature construction uses a different restricted or chirality-modified operator.
fate: The general spectral-flow theorem is \citet[\S7]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3}; its signature discussion in \S6 uses the appropriate signature operator. The notebook does not record the missing modification. The chapter’s grading-symmetry verification explains why its ungraded example cannot supply a nonzero obstruction.
present_status: As of November 2026, the vanishing is an elementary consequence of parity symmetry. The intended nontrivial example cannot be recovered merely by citing the general index theorem.
reconstruction: \ours\ The parity-symmetry deduction is supplied here and proved in the chapter’s verification subsection. It diagnoses the literal recorded example; it does not reconstruct an unrecorded operator restriction.

title: The incomplete higher-signature example
notes: The page mentions characters \(\pi_1(X)\to\mathbb Z\to S^1\), \(X^{4k+1}\times S^1\), Novikov’s invariant, and Hirzebruch’s \(L\)-polynomial.
statement: A family of flat line-bundle twists over a character circle can be paired with an odd elliptic symbol through an index theorem. The notes do not specify a signature-type operator, its grading, the twisting bundle on the product, or the precise cohomology pairing. Therefore no unique higher-signature formula follows from the recorded data.
fate: \citet[\S\S5--7]{atiyahpatodisinger1976spectral3} provides related index formulas for flat bundles and signature operators. The match here is thematic, unlike the exact identification of item 1971-237.4. A dimensional or grading repair must not be silently attributed to Atiyah’s unrecorded speech.
present_status: As of November 2026, the general subject is developed, but this particular compressed example remains incompletely identifiable. The literal \(d+\delta\) interpretation has the zero-flow limitation just explained.

title: Motives and different cohomology theories: no recorded result
notes: The entry reads Deligne, in Manin’s translation, on the theory of motives and different cohomology theories of algebraic varieties.
statement: The text supports only this subject identification. It gives no category of motives, equivalence relation on algebraic cycles, realization functor, or conjectural comparison that could be made into a uniquely attributable theorem.
fate: No specific publication is assigned. Attaching the Weil conjectures or a later motivic theory would fill a gap with information not contained in the notes.
present_status: As of November 2026, the entry remains a subject notice; this is insufficient evidence for any claim about the fate of a particular mathematical problem.

title: Schubert cells in a complex Grassmannian
notes: The notes choose \(a_1\le\cdots\le a_n\le N\), a complete flag \(E_j\), and jumps \(a_i+i\) for \(\dim(F\cap E_j)\).
statement: For \(\operatorname{Gr}(n,\mathbb C^N)\), choose \(0\le a_1\le\cdots\le a_n\le N-n\). The corresponding Schubert cell consists of planes whose intersection-dimension function jumps precisely at \(b_i=a_i+i\); it is an affine space of complex dimension \(\sum_i a_i\). The closure is defined by the associated rank inequalities and is a projective Schubert variety.
fate: The notebook explicitly cites \citet{horrocks1957schubert}, published in 1957. The geometry and its indexing are also checked in \citet[\S4]{tamvakis2004connection}; his quotient-bundle convention is transposed from the usual subspace convention and should not be copied without translation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the affine decomposition is established. Requiring equality only at a few selected flag dimensions, without the complete jump data, does not specify the open cell.

title: Schubert cycles give an integral homology basis
notes: The cell decomposition is used to compare bases in homology and cohomology.
statement: The closures of the complex Schubert cells give a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of the homology of the Grassmannian. The affine cells have even real dimensions, so the cellular boundary maps vanish and odd homology is zero. A cohomology basis is obtained by Poincaré duality, with complementary rather than equal complex dimensions.
fate: This is classical Schubert calculus underlying \citet{horrocks1957schubert}; \citet[\S4]{tamvakis2004connection} makes the cycle/cohomology conventions explicit. The seminar is expository.
present_status: As of November 2026, the integral assertion is established, stronger than a real de Rham basis. Open noncompact cells themselves are not ordinary compact integration cycles.

title: Basic invariant forms on the homogeneous quotient
notes: The Grassmannian is \(U(N)/(U(n)\times U(N-n))\). Forms are lifted to \(U(N)\); the first descent condition is written as vanishing when the listed arguments lie in the subgroup tangent space.
statement: For a principal \(H\)-bundle \(G\to G/H\), a differential form descends precisely when it is \(H\)-invariant and horizontal: insertion of any one vertical tangent vector gives zero. Vanishing only when all arguments are vertical is insufficient in degree greater than one. Invariant forms on the Grassmannian are the \(H\)-invariant alternating tensors on \(\mathfrak g/\mathfrak h\).
fate: This is the basic-form construction behind the Chern--Weil treatment in \citet[\S3]{tamvakis2004connection}, tracing the classical work of Chern, Weil, and Cartan. The descent criterion is older than the talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the criterion is established. The notebook’s compressed first condition must be read in the stronger insertion sense for its later construction to work.

title: The curvature matrix and invariant characteristic forms
notes: The Maurer--Cartan entries \(\theta_{jk}\) are used in \(\Theta_{jk}=-(2\pi i)^{-1}\sum_s\theta_{js}\wedge\overline{\Theta}_{ks}\); the second factor is marked graphically uncertain. Conjugation-invariant polynomials in this matrix descend to the Grassmannian.
statement: For the tautological Hermitian bundle or its dual, the induced connection has a curvature matrix whose entries are sums of wedges of two off-diagonal Maurer--Cartan one-forms. In a compatible convention the displayed second factor must be \(\overline\theta_{ks}\), so the result has degree two. A degree-\(r\) invariant polynomial in normalized curvature is a closed \(2r\)-form with connection-independent cohomology class.
fate: This is classical Chern--Weil theory, explicitly reviewed in \citet[\S3 and \S4]{tamvakis2004connection}. The scan does not conclusively distinguish upper- and lower-case theta in the uncertain factor; degree counting gives the mathematical emendation, not paleographic certainty.
present_status: As of November 2026, the curvature construction is established. The sign depends on whether the tautological bundle, quotient, or dual is used; that choice must be made before identifying its Chern or Schur class.
reconstruction: The lower-case second factor is a mathematical reconstruction. The case uncertainty is preserved in the corrections rather than called a proven transcription error.

title: The alternant quotient as a Schur polynomial and character
notes: A quotient of determinants with exponents \(\lambda_n,\lambda_{n-1}+1,\ldots,\lambda_1+n-1\) is said to be a polynomial and the character of the representation with highest weight \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0\).
statement: For a partition \(\lambda\) of length at most \(n\), \(s_\lambda(x)=\det(x_i^{\lambda_j+n-j})/\det(x_i^{n-j})\) extends to a symmetric polynomial, including repeated eigenvalues. It is the character of the irreducible polynomial representation of \(GL_n\) with highest weight \(\lambda\). Substituting a matrix of commuting even-degree forms is interpreted through the polynomial, not by dividing differential forms.
fate: The representation-theoretic identity is classical and is the algebraic input of \citet{horrocks1957schubert}. \citet[\S2]{tamvakis2004connection} verifies the Schur functor and invariant-polynomial interpretation directly.
present_status: As of November 2026, the formula is established. The notebook’s reversed order of determinant columns gives the same quotient because numerator and denominator acquire the same sign.

title: Schur curvature forms and the dual Schubert basis
notes: The notes substitute curvature into the Schur polynomial, put \(a_i=N-n-\lambda_i\), and assert integral one over the corresponding Schubert cell and zero over the others; form degree is equated with cell dimension.
statement: In the standard subspace convention, let \(S\) be the rank-\(n\) tautological bundle and let \(\lambda\) fit the \(n\times(N-n)\) rectangle. The Schur class \(s_\lambda(S^*)\) is the Schubert cohomology class \(\sigma_\lambda\) of degree \(2|\lambda|\). If \(\lambda^\vee_i=N-n-\lambda_{n+1-i}\), then \(\int_{[\Omega_\mu]}\sigma_\lambda=\delta_{\mu,\lambda^\vee}\) for \(|\mu|=n(N-n)-|\lambda|\). Integrate over closed Schubert cycles, with consistent indexing and real degree.
fate: This is the Schur-form/Schubert-class relation of \citet{horrocks1957schubert}; a complete modern formulation is \citet[Theorem 1, \S4]{tamvakis2004connection}. The notebook’s displayed indexing conflates the cycle Poincaré-dual to a class with the cycle on which that class evaluates to one.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected duality statement is established. The literal formula is generally dimensionally inconsistent unless the partition and cycle are complemented appropriately.
reconstruction: The dual bundle and standard partition convention are fixed here explicitly; the notebook’s uncertain \(N^{\prime}\) is not interpreted as a new ambient dimension.

title: Gelfand’s unspecified request to describe a modular group algebra
notes: I. M. Gelfand asks to describe the group ring of \(SL_2(\mathbb F_q)\) with coefficients in the algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F_q\).
statement: The object is \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q[SL_2(\mathbb F_q)]\), in the defining characteristic. The word \emph{describe} does not specify whether one seeks simple modules, blocks, the Jacobson radical, a presentation, indecomposables, or a Morita-equivalent algebra. These are different questions. Since the characteristic divides the group order, a semisimple character decomposition alone does not describe this algebra.
fate: The object is identifiable but the requested invariant is not. Searches of modular \(SL_2\) group-algebra descriptions did not turn this wording into one uniquely matchable problem, so no theorem about simple representations is substituted for a full algebra classification.
present_status: As of November 2026, this occurrence remains an underdetermined request, not a certified unsolved problem. It receives no new problem-index identifier because no definite target is stated.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Algebraic order of a differential operator
notes: Vinogradov proposes an algebraic theory over any ring, explicitly allowing a noncommutative ring. For an additive map \(A:M\to N\), the notes define \((kA)m=kA(m)\), \((k^+A)m=A(km)\), and \(\delta_k=k^+-k\); order at most \(n\) means every \((n+1)\)-fold iterated \(\delta\) vanishes.
statement: Let \(K\) be a commutative unital algebra over a commutative base \(R\), and let \(M,N\) be unital \(K\)-modules. An \(R\)-linear map \(A:M\to N\) has order at most \(n\) when \(\delta_{k_0}\cdots\delta_{k_n}A=0\) for all \(k_j\in K\). Order zero means \(K\)-linearity. Additive operators correspond to the base \(R=\mathbb Z\). For a noncommutative ring these same formulas do not furnish the ensuing commutative two-module calculus without additional choices.
fate: The commutator definition predates this lecture: \citet[\S16.8]{grothendieck1967egaiv4} was published in 1967. The closely matching presentation in \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic}, received 19 January 1972, explicitly assumes a commutative ring with identity; that hypothesis is essential to its subsequent functors.
present_status: As of November 2026, the commutative definition is standard. Noncommutative differential calculi require a specified replacement; the notebook’s unrestricted wording is not a theorem extending the entire construction.

title: Agreement with differential operators on vector bundles
notes: The notes state that the algebraic definition agrees with the classical one.
statement: For a smooth finite-dimensional manifold \(X\), take \(K=C^\infty(X,\mathbb R)\), \(R=\mathbb R\), and \(M=\Gamma(E),N=\Gamma(F)\) for smooth finite-rank vector bundles. The \(\mathbb R\)-linear operators satisfying the iterated-commutator criterion of order at most \(n\) are exactly the usual linear differential operators of that order. This assertion concerns section modules, not arbitrary algebraic modules over \(C^\infty(X)\).
fate: \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic} states this comparison as part of the announced programme; \citet[Theorem 2.2]{vinogradov2015logic} restates it. The classical differential operators themselves were already familiar; Class A concerns this lecture’s published algebraic presentation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the comparison is established under the stated smooth hypotheses. Identification of every universal algebraic form with an ordinary smooth form requires a further category restriction, discussed in occurrence 1971-241.3.

title: Cojet corepresentation and its evaluation operator
notes: The right module \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(M,N)\) is written as \(\operatorname{Hom}_K(M,\operatorname{Diff}_n^+N)\), with \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+N=\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(K,N)\). The latter object is called cojets.
statement: For commutative unital \(K/R\), put \(C_n(N)=\operatorname{Diff}_{K/R,n}(K,N)\) with scalar action \((a\cdot B)(b)=B(ab)\). There is a natural \(K\)-module isomorphism \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(M,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_K(M,C_n(N))\), given by \(A\mapsto[m\mapsto(b\mapsto A(bm))]\). Its inverse is composition with \(\epsilon(B)=B(1)\), an operator of order at most \(n\).
fate: This exact cojet formulation is printed in \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic}. The November 8 continuation supplies its proof in six elementary lemmas, recorded separately as occurrences 1971-242.1--6.
present_status: As of November 2026, the natural isomorphism is established. The precomposition action is indispensable: replacing it by pointwise multiplication would make the displayed currying map generally nonlinear over \(K\).

title: Jets represent differential operators in the target variable
notes: The notes pair the cojet formula with \(\operatorname{Diff}_n(M,N)=\operatorname{Hom}(J^n(M),N)\) and announce existence of jets.
statement: For commutative \(K/R\), a universal map \(j_n:M\to J^n_{K/R}(M)\) of order at most \(n\) induces \(\operatorname{Hom}_K(J^n_{K/R}(M),N)\cong\operatorname{Diff}_{K/R,n}(M,N)\) naturally in \(N\). Here the operator module uses multiplication on its values. Existence follows from the quotient construction written explicitly in the next lecture; no finite generation or projectivity is required for algebraic module representability.
fate: Principal parts and their universal property are older, in \citet[\S16.8]{grothendieck1967egaiv4}. \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic} places the two universal properties side by side. The construction is expository as a representability fact.
present_status: As of November 2026, the algebraic universal property is established. Being a finite-rank geometric jet bundle is a stronger smooth or regularity statement.

title: The algebra generated by the two scalar actions
notes: The notes suggest constructing \(J^n(K)\) as the algebra generated by \(k\) and \(k^+\) on \(\operatorname{Diff}_nK\); a lower index in the formula remains uncertain.
statement: The canonical algebraic construction is \(J^n_{K/R}(K)=(K\otimes_R K)/I^{n+1}\), where \(I=\ker(K\otimes_RK\to K)\). The two factors give the two scalar actions and their differences generate \(I\). An action of this quotient on an operator module need not be faithful, so identifying the universal algebra with its image on one chosen module needs a separate argument.
fate: This is the principal-parts construction of \citet[\S16.8]{grothendieck1967egaiv4}; the jet quotient is also given in \citet[Proposition 7.1]{vinogradov2015logic}. Neither source justifies an unrestricted faithfulness claim for the notebook’s chosen representation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the universal quotient is established; the exact intended lower index and whether equality with an operator image was meant remain uncertain.
reconstruction: The diagonal-ideal quotient is a mathematical reconstruction, not a claimed reading of the crossed notation.

title: Recursive multiderivation functors
notes: Before the 1 November heading, the notes define \(D_1(N)=\operatorname{Der}(K,N)\), explain that it is a left submodule but only a subset of \(\operatorname{Diff}_1^+N\), and put \(D_i(N)=D\{D_{i-1}(N)\subset(\operatorname{Diff}_1^+)^{i-1}N\}\).
statement: For a subset \(S\) of a \(K\)-module \(Q\), write \(D(S\subset Q)\) for the \(R\)-derivations \(K\to Q\) whose values lie in \(S\). Starting with \(D_0(N)=N\), the notebook’s recursive definition uses the indicated precomposition module at each stage. It cannot be replaced by repeated application of the ordinary left-module functor \(D\). In the smooth geometric category it produces multivector fields with coefficients in \(N\).
fate: The recursive construction and the warning that the intermediate subset is not a right submodule appear in \citet[\S2]{vinogradov1972logic}; the later explanation is \citet[\S5.2]{vinogradov2015logic}.
present_status: As of November 2026, this construction is established in the commutative setting. Its representing objects are forms; the functor values are multiderivations, a distinction blurred in the next lecture.

title: Repeated commutators recover the Hamilton–Jacobi symbol
notes: The 1 November entry calls \(\delta_f\cdots\delta_f\mathcal D\), with the same function everywhere, the left side of a Hamilton--Jacobi equation, and asks the audience to calculate it.
statement: For a scalar differential operator \(A=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha(x)\partial^\alpha\) over a smooth real manifold, use the symbol convention \(\sigma_m(A)(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha\), without factors of \(i\). Let \(m_f\) denote multiplication by \(f\), and define \(\delta_fA=[A,m_f]=A\circ m_f-m_f\circ A\). Then \(\delta_f^mA\) is multiplication by \(m!\,\sigma_m(A)(x,df_x)\). Thus the leading characteristic phase equation is \(\sigma_m(A)(x,df_x)=0\). Repeated commutators over a general ring need not permit division by \(m!\).
fate: \citet[\S7]{vinogradov1972logic} publishes the symbol/Hamiltonian part of this programme in 1972. The principal-symbol and Hamilton--Jacobi concepts are older; Class A records the algebraic reformulation anticipated by this exercise, not a claim of priority for those concepts.
present_status: As of November 2026, the scalar smooth identity is established and elementary. A Hamilton--Jacobi equation for a system or an inhomogeneous problem requires an additional specified principal-symbol equation.
reconstruction: \ours The precise normalization follows by applying the product rule \(m\) times: all lower-order terms disappear and each top-order derivative contributes the corresponding symmetric product of \(df\), with \(m!\) permutations.

title: The tensor-quotient construction of universal jets
notes: The notes write \(J^s(M)=(K\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)/\Pi_s\), where \(\Pi_s\) is generated by \((\bar k_0-k_0)\cdots(\bar k_s-k_s)\) applied to tensors.
statement: For commutative \(K/R\), give \(K\otimes_R M\) the two actions \(a(b\otimes m)=ab\otimes m\) and \(\bar a(b\otimes m)=b\otimes am\). Let \(\Pi_s\) be the submodule generated by every \((\bar a_0-a_0)\cdots(\bar a_s-a_s)(b\otimes m)\). The quotient with \(j_s(m)=[1\otimes m]\) represents order-\(s\) operators: \(A\) corresponds to the unique homomorphism \([b\otimes m]\mapsto bA(m)\).
fate: This is the older principal-parts universal construction, in \citet[\S16.8]{grothendieck1967egaiv4}; the lecture’s exact module form is restated in \citet[Proposition 7.1]{vinogradov2015logic}. The \(\mathbb Z\)-tensor in the notes correctly corresponds to additive, absolute operators.
present_status: As of November 2026, the quotient construction works without smoothness, finite generation, or freeness. The base ring must remain fixed when one compares it with relative differential operators.

title: Which universal forms recover ordinary smooth forms?
notes: The representing modules \(\Lambda_i\) are identified with ordinary differential forms, while all \(K\)-modules are apparently allowed.
statement: An identification with the ordinary smooth cotangent and exterior-form modules requires the geometric category over \(C^\infty(X)\), or an equivalent smooth-module universal property. Universal algebraic Kähler differentials representing derivations into every algebraic module can be larger. The distinction does not invalidate the differential-operator comparison for finite-rank bundle sections.
fate: \citet[Proposition 7.2 and Example 7.1]{vinogradov2015logic} explicitly separates the two categories; its example warns that algebraic differentiation of \(e^x\) need not satisfy the ordinary smooth chain rule in the unrestricted universal module. This clarifies a suppressed hypothesis in the 1971 account.
present_status: As of November 2026, the geometric-category reconstruction is established. Calling the unrestricted representing objects ordinary smooth forms is not literally correct.

title: Skew multiderivations and the distinction from covariant forms
notes: The repeated derivation calculation yields \(D(a)(b)+D(b)(a)=0\). The notes then call \(D_k(M)\) \emph{\(k\)-forms with values in \(M\)}. In the two-coordinate calculation, several coefficients multiplying \(b\) are followed by \(\partial_x\) rather than \(\partial_y\).
statement: The recursive objects are multiderivations. If 2 is invertible in the base, their skew symmetry gives alternating maps, and \(D_k(M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_K(\bigwedge^k\Omega^1_{K/R},M)\). Over a smooth real manifold, with geometric modules, these are multivector fields with coefficients in \(M\); \(\Lambda_k\), the representing covariant object, is the form module. In characteristic two, skew symmetry alone does not impose alternation.
fate: \citet[\S2]{vinogradov1972logic} publishes the recursive functors; \citet[\S5.2]{vinogradov2015logic} explicitly calls their smooth realizations multivector fields. The variance distinction repairs the notebook’s terminology.
present_status: As of November 2026, the characteristic-zero interpretation is established. The characteristic-two examples must be examined with their exact functor and differential, rather than silently importing ordinary exterior powers.

title: The claimed nonzero second functor over the prime field
notes: The bottom line reads \(K=\mathbb Z_2\), \(D_2\ne0\), followed by a parenthesis referring to second de Rham cohomology.
statement: If \(\mathbb Z_2\) denotes the field \(\mathbb F_2\), the literal claim is false for the stated additive-derivation functors: every derivation from \(\mathbb F_2\) to a unital module is zero, so \(D_i(M)=0\) for every \(i\ge1\). A nonreduced algebra such as \(\mathbb F_2[C_2]\), considered on the next page, is a different object. Nonzero \(D_2\) is also not the same assertion as nonzero second cohomology.
fate: No matching published statement was identified in the examined 1972 announcement or later survey. Their definitions suffice to reject the literal prime-field example; the neighbouring group-algebra example is a possible source of compression, not a justified silent substitution.
present_status: As of November 2026, the literal prime-field assertion is refuted. The intended alternative example and the parenthetical identification remain unverified.
reconstruction: \ours A derivation satisfies \(D(1)=D(1\cdot1)=2D(1)\), hence \(D(1)=0\); additivity then makes it zero on the prime field. Induction in the notebook’s definition gives the higher vanishing.

title: The group-ring/de Rham comparison is not identified
notes: For the group algebra of the two-element group over \(\mathbb Z_2\), the notes claim all de Rham cohomology groups are \(\mathbb Z_2\), then assert that de Rham cohomology of group rings equals group cohomology. They contrast this with the diagonal-ideal definition of classical forms.
statement: The claim requires a specified complex and coefficient convention. For ordinary exterior Kähler forms of \(A=\mathbb F_2[C_2]\cong\mathbb F_2[y]/(y^2)\), one obtains \(H^0_{\rm dR}(A/\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2\), \(H^1_{\rm dR}(A/\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2\), and zero in higher degrees. Thus this ordinary complex cannot realize the stated nonzero group in every degree. A different recursively defined characteristic-two complex cannot be identified solely from that numerical claim.
fate: English and Russian searches for the group-ring comparison, and examination of \citet{vinogradov1972logic,vinogradov2015logic}, did not locate a theorem matching the unrestricted assertion. Its relation to later algebraic de Rham constructions remains unidentified.
present_status: As of November 2026, no exact publication match for the notebook’s alternative theory is claimed. The ordinary de Rham interpretation is false; this does not establish that every conceivable corrected comparison fails.
reconstruction: \ours For the stated ordinary complex, \(\Omega^1=A\,dy\), \(\Omega^i=0\) for \(i\ge2\), and \(d(a+by)=b\,dy\). Its kernel and cokernel give the displayed calculation. This is an editorial diagnostic, not a computation of the unidentified alternative complex.

title: Representation of multiderivations by universal forms
notes: The lecture announces existence of \(\Lambda_i(K)\) with \(D_i(M)=\operatorname{Hom}_K(\Lambda_i(K),M)\).
statement: In the commutative algebraic setting, the multiderivation functors are represented by universal modules. Over a base in which 2 is invertible, the standard alternating interpretation gives \(\Lambda_i(K)=\bigwedge^i\Omega^1_{K/R}\), with \(\Lambda_0=K\). Over general rings the exact skew-versus-alternating convention must be retained. Universal objects for a restricted smooth category are taken in that category.
fate: The announcement \citet[\S5]{vinogradov1972logic} gives the representing-module formulation; \citet[\S7.2]{vinogradov2015logic} makes category dependence explicit. Kähler differentials and exterior powers themselves are older constructions.
present_status: As of November 2026, the universal-property formulation is established. It does not identify multiderivations themselves with covariant forms, nor erase the characteristic-two distinction.

title: The exterior differential from a natural transformation
notes: The inclusion \(D_i\to D_{i-1}(\operatorname{Diff}_1^+)\) is translated through universal objects into a first-order operator \(d:\Lambda_{i-1}\to\Lambda_i\). The notes check that consecutive compositions vanish.
statement: In the commutative setting with a consistent form convention, the natural transformation is represented by a map \(J^1(\Lambda_{i-1})\to\Lambda_i\); composing with the universal jet gives \(d\). For ordinary alternating forms, \(d(a_0\,da_1\wedge\cdots\wedge da_i)=da_0\wedge da_1\wedge\cdots\wedge da_i\), which gives \(d^2=0\). The differential is first order over \(K\), generally not \(K\)-linear.
fate: This natural-transformation construction is published in \citet[\S5]{vinogradov1972logic}; the representative/jet mechanism is restated in \citet[\S7.2]{vinogradov2015logic}. Class A concerns the categorical construction rather than the classical existence of \(d\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the de Rham complex is established. Its cohomology depends on the ring, base, and module category; the disputed group-ring claim is not a consequence of representability alone.

title: Finite and stable algebraic Spencer complexes
notes: Composition of operators and the functor inclusions give \(D_{i+1}(\operatorname{Diff}_k^+M)\to D_i(\operatorname{Diff}_{k+1}^+M)\). The finite and direct-limit chains are called a Spencer resolution, followed by the more cautious statement \emph{this is a complex}.
statement: For each total order \(r\), the terms \(D_i(\operatorname{Diff}_{r-i}^+M)\) form a complex ending in \(\operatorname{Diff}_r^+M\to M\), with augmentation evaluation at 1. Taking the filtered union of finite-order operator modules gives the stable complex. For arbitrary commutative rings these complexes need not be exact; extra regularity and category assumptions are required to call them resolutions.
fate: \citet[\S3]{vinogradov1972logic} explicitly states that its finite complex is exact in the last two terms, that the order-one complex is exact, and that higher complexes need not be exact. The smooth antecedent is \citet{spencer1969overdetermined}; the new feature is the functorial algebraic framework.
present_status: As of November 2026, the complexes and their possible nonzero homology are established. The notebook’s universal word \emph{resolution} must be qualified; its later word \emph{complex} is the valid unrestricted assertion.

title: An index over an arbitrary ring is only a programme heading
notes: The concluding headings include \emph{the index over any ring}. No index group, admissible class of operators, or finiteness condition is given.
statement: A mathematical index theorem here would need a defined class of operators, a target group for the index, hypotheses making the relevant kernel/cokernel or homological classes meaningful, and a comparison with a symbol construction. The notebook does not specify these data, so it does not pose one unique general theorem.
fate: \citet[\S4 and concluding remarks of \S7]{vinogradov1972logic} relates Spencer homology to kernels and cokernels under acyclicity assumptions and announces a later algebraic index generalization. That is a concrete partial programme, but not a verified all-rings index theorem matching the bare heading.
present_status: As of November 2026, the occurrence remains insufficiently specified for a separate problem-index entry or a claim of current openness. No blanket general index theorem is inferred from later uses of the same terminology.

title: Hamiltonian formalism over a commutative algebra
notes: The final list also promises a Hamiltonian formalism \emph{for every ring}.
